ARCHIVE: The Clinton administration Middle East policy was heavily shaped by officials with close ties to Israel or to prominent pro-Israel organizations. The two most notable individuals were Martin Indyk and Dennis Ross. Indyk was former deputy director of research at AIPAC. He cofounded the pro-Israel Washington Institute for Near East Policy. He served on Clinton National Security Council, as ambassador to Israel (1995 to 1997 and 2000 to 2001), and as assistant secretary of state (1997 to 2000). Dennis Ross served as Clinton special envoy to the Middle East. He joined WINEP after leaving government in 2001. Both were among President Clinton closest advisers at the Camp David summit in July 2000. Indyk and Ross supported Oslo peace process and favored creation of a Palestinian state. But they did so only within limits of what would be acceptable to Israeli leaders. The American delegation at Camp David took most of its cues from Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak. It coordinated negotiating positions with Israel in advance. It did not offer its own independent proposals for settling the conflict. Even the Clinton parameters presented in December 2000 were less an independent American proposal. They were Clinton summary of where negotiations stood and his assessment of bargaining space within which a solution might be found. Palestinian negotiators complained about this. Israelis would sometimes present them with a specific proposal. Later the Americans would offer the same idea. But Americans would label it a "bridging proposal." Another member of US team later admitted Israeli proposals were often "presented [to the Palestinians] as U.S. concepts, not Israeli ones." This subterfuge fooled no one and reinforced Palestinian suspicions. Palestinian representatives protested that they were "negotiating with two Israeli teams—one displaying an Israeli flag, and one an American flag." So the US negotiators served Israel position, not America own. They presented Israeli demands as American ideas to the Palestinians. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: In 1992 New York businessman Haim Katz called AIPAC President David Steiner pretending to be a potential donor. Katz secretly taped the call. Steiner described how AIPAC helped direct campaign contributions to friendly politicians. He also said he met personally to "cut a deal" with Secretary of State James Baker for $3 billion in foreign aid to Israel. Plus "a billion dollars in other goodies that people dont even know about." More to the point Steiner told Katz "we have a dozen people in [Clinton's] campaign, in the headquarters... and theyre all going to get big jobs." Steiner was forced to resign after Katz went public. He later said his statements were not true. But the authors say there is little reason to doubt the thrust of his remarks. AIPAC also vetted presidential advisers. In 1987 former AIPAC head Tom Dine told an interviewer "This is an actual example... One of the [1988] presidential candidates called us and said I will be publicly declaring soon, and I am interested in hiring so and so for a top campaign position. Tell me what you think about him." Dine said his answer was thumbs up in that case. Jimmy Carter wanted George Ball as his first secretary of state. But he knew Ball was perceived as critical of Israel and that the lobby would oppose the appointment. Richard Marius was a Harvard lecturer hired in 1995 as Vice President Al Gore chief speechwriter. He said he was fired before he began work. This happened after New Republic publisher Martin Peretz falsely claimed Marius was an anti-Semite based on a book review Marius published in 1992. In 2001 Bruce Riedel left his position handling Middle East issues on National Security Council. The New Republic reported that Pentagon held up appointment of Riedel designated successor Alina Romanowski. Pentagon officials suspected her of being "insufficiently supportive of the Jewish state." So the lobby does not only lobby. It decides who gets key jobs in the US government. And it blocks people it sees as critical of Israel. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: In the 2004 presidential campaign Howard Dean made a mistake. He recommended that the United States take a more "even-handed role" in the Arab-Israeli conflict. One of Dean rivals for the nomination was Joseph Lieberman. Lieberman accused Dean of selling Israel down the river. He labeled Dean statement "irresponsible." Even more remarkably virtually all of the top Democrats in the House of Representatives signed a hard-hitting letter to Dean criticizing his comments. The Chicago Jewish Star reported that "anonymous attackers... are clogging the e-mail inboxes of Jewish leaders around the country, warning—without much evidence—that Dean would somehow be bad for Israel." This worry was absurd. Dean is in fact an unabashed supporter of Israel. His campaign cochair was former AIPAC president Steven Grossman. Dean said his own views on the Middle East more closely reflected those of AIPAC than the more moderate Americans for Peace Now. Dean wife is Jewish and his children were raised Jewish as well. Dean was not questioning US support for Israel. He had merely suggested that to "bring the sides together" Washington should act as an honest broker. This is not a radical idea. But key groups in the lobby do not welcome the idea of evenhandedness when it comes to the Arab-Israeli conflict. Dean failure to win the Democratic nomination has many causes. But the incident underscored the potential cost of being anything less than ardently pro-Israel during a presidential campaign. So the lobby punishes even a mild call for America to act as honest broker. This shows US presidents and candidates cannot take an independent position on Israel. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Groups in the Israel lobby exert significant leverage over the executive branch. Influence over the executive branch derives in part from the impact pro-Israel voters and donors have on presidential elections. Pro-Israel donors are a small part of the population. But they make large campaign donations to candidates from both parties. Hamilton Jordan was presidential adviser and former White House Chief of Staff. He wrote in a confidential memo to President Jimmy Carter: "Wherever there is major political fundraising in this country, you will find American Jews playing a significant role." The Washington Post once estimated that Democratic presidential candidates "depend on Jewish supporters to supply as much as 60 percent of the money raised from private sources." Other estimates are lower. But pro-Israel contributions form a substantial share, between 20 and 50 percent, of the contributions made to the Democratic party and its presidential candidates. Israel is not the only issue that inspires these contributions. But candidates who are perceived as hostile, or even indifferent, to Israel run the risk of seeing some of these funds go to their opponents. Pro-Israel voters also have high turnout rates. They are concentrated in key states like California, Florida, Illinois, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania. This increases their weight in determining who becomes president. In close races this vote can tip the balance in key states. Jeffrey Helmreich of the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs wrote that "American Jewish voters maintain the potential to be the decisive factor in national election results... American Jews wield power through their high concentration in key states and their tendency to behave as a swing vote." Because this vote matters in close elections, presidential candidates go to considerable lengths to cultivate support. Candidates are especially eager to appeal to AIPAC and other organizations in the lobby. They know that the seal of approval from these prominent organizations will facilitate fund-raising and encourage higher turnout on their behalf. Gaining and retaining that support means backing Israel down the line. This happens even though Israel strategic value has declined. It also happens even though some Israeli actions, like the continued effort to colonize the Occupied Territories, are at odds with stated US policy. So the lobby uses American campaign money and American election mechanics to make US presidents back Israel. This happens against America own stated policy. ARCHIVE: AIPAC traditional tactics to influence Congress also enable the lobby to put pressure on the executive branch. This happens when the executive takes actions considered not in Israel interest. When that happens the president or cabinet official is likely to get a hard-hitting letter from one or both houses of Congress. The letter is signed by most of its members. President Gerald Ford got such a letter in 1975 when he threatened a reassessment of US-Israeli relations. President Bush got a similar letter in April 2002 when he briefly sought to pressure Israel to end a large-scale military incursion in the Occupied Territories. The lopsided percentage of signatories for each of these letters is eloquent testimony to AIPAC ability to twist arms. Senator Daniel Inouye (D-HI) commented after signing the letter to Ford in 1975: "It is easier to sign one letter than to answer 5000." Senator John Culver (D-IA) later admitted: "The pressure was just too great. I caved." Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice felt the same pressure. She sought to restart the peace process by visiting the Middle East in March 2007. Just before her departure Rice received an AIPAC-sponsored letter signed by seventy-nine senators. The letter urged her to avoid contact with the new Palestinian unity government until it recognized Israel, renounced terror, and agreed to abide by Israeli-Palestinian agreements. Former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger once told AIPAC Tom Dine: "Dine, I deal with you because you could hurt me." AIPAC bills itself as America Pro-Israel Lobby. It has an almost unchallenged hold on Congress. One of the three main branches of the American government is firmly committed to supporting Israel. Open debate about US policy toward Israel does not occur there even though that policy has important consequences for the entire world. Senator Ernest Hollings (D-SC) noted as he was leaving office in 2004: "You cant have an Israeli policy other than what AIPAC gives you around here." Another senator speaking on condition of anonymity told a Washington Post reporter in 1991: "My colleagues think AIPAC is a very, very powerful organization that is ruthless, and very, very alert. Eighty percent of the senators here roll their eyes on some of the votes. They know that what they are doing isnt what they really believe is right, but why fight on a situation where they are liable to get beat up on?" Former Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon once told an American audience: "When people ask me how they can help Israel, I tell them—Help AIPAC." His successor Ehud Olmert agrees remarking: "Thank God we have AIPAC, the greatest supporter and friend we have in the whole world." Quel statut pour les citoyens français vivant à Jérusalem-Est et en Judée-Samarie (Cisjordanie) ? Par Michel Calvo, [15 novembre 2026] La reconnaissance par la France de l’État de Palestine à Gaza, en Cisjordanie et à Jérusalem Est entraîne plusieurs conséquences dont tout haut fonctionnaire devrait pouvoir anticiper les effets. L’absence de coordination de nos dirigeants actuels est, à cet égard, pour le moins préoccupante. La décision de reconnaissance de la Palestine a été prise en période de gouvernement démissionnaire par un Président de la République incompétent pour en décider seul. À cela s’ajoute de manque de respect des engagements internationaux pris par la France. Aujourd’hui le Consulat de Belgique a Jérusalem refuse de donner des services consulaires aux Belges (juifs) qui résident à Jérusalem Est et en Cisjordanie… La France va-t-elle en faire autant ? Selon mon passeport français, je suis un Français vivant à l’étranger, à Jérusalem, mais la France ne reconnaît pas Jérusalem comme une ville située en Israël… Je n’habite donc dans aucun pays, selon mon passeport français… Mon passeport français ne mentionne aucunement Israël comme pays où je réside . La France considère depuis 1947, que tout Jérusalem et Bethlehem constituent un « Corpus Separatum » (un corps séparé) placé sous un régime international spécial, régime qui n’a jamais vu le jour. .. La France se fonde sur la résolution 181 de 1947 de l’Assemblée Générale des Nations Unies qui proposait d’internationaliser Jérusalem et ses environs (y compris Bethléem), dans le cadre du plan de partage de la Palestine. Cette proposition n’a pas été suivie d’effet, les États arabes/musulmans l’ayant rejetée. La France ne peut donc pas l’invoquer. Jusqu’à la reconnaissance par la France de l’État de Palestine, j’étais considéré comme résident de l’État d’Israël dans des domaines précis. C’est le cas de tous les français résidant à Jérusalem (dans tout Jérusalem) et en Cisjordanie, dont le nombre s’élève entre 7 000 et 13.000. Jusqu’à la reconnaissance par la France de l’État de Palestine, j’ai été considéré, comme tous les Français vivant à Jérusalem et en Judée Samarie/Cisjordanie, comme résident fiscal de l’État d’Israël. La Convention fiscale du 31 juillet 1996 a été conclue entre la France et Israël en vue d’éviter la double imposition, et de prévenir l’évasion fiscale en matière d’impôts sur le revenu et sur la fortune. En vertu de cette convention, je suis considéré par la France comme résident en Israël, bien que sur mon passeport Israël ne soit pas mentionné. En conséquence, ma pension n’est imposée qu’en Israël. Du fait de la reconnaissance de l’État de Palestine par la France, JE DEVIENS LOGIQUEMENT POUR LA FRANCE UN RÉSIDENT FISCAL DE L’ÉTAT DE PALESTINE. En l’absence de Convention fiscale entre la France et la Palestine en vue d’éviter les doubles impositions, Mes pensions seront imposées en France. Israël pouvant contester mon statut de résident de Palestine, pourra exiger que ma pension soit assujettie aux impôts sur le revenu en Israël puisque, pour elle, j’y réside. La Palestine pourra aussi exiger de lui payer des impôts, à moins qu’elle n’expulse tous ses Juifs. Ne peuvent être résidents de Palestine que les Juifs qui y habitaient avant 1948, selon son projet de constitution. Je vais donc devoir payer des impôts dans deux pays, France et Israël et peut être en Palestine. La situation est la même pour tous les citoyens français vivant sur le territoire de la Palestine (Judée Samarie, anciennement dénommée par la France Cisjordanie)… J’ai soulevé cette question au Service des impôts. La question a été transférée à Bercy semble-t-il. À ce jour elle demeure sans réponse. Une situation similaire résulte de la Convention en matière de Sécurité Sociale entre le Gouvernement de l’État d’Israël et le Gouvernement de la République Française du 17 décembre 1966. Cette convention vise à coordonner l’application aux ressortissants français et israéliens de la législation française sur la sécurité sociale et de la législation israélienne sur l’assurance nationale. Hello comrades. First of all we want to share our self-criticism for the late reporting of this month. Now, already in mid November, some new developments took place already, not so much in Rojava but in other parts in Kurdistan. We will also report about it here. ----------------------------------------------------------------- Monthly higlights, October 2026 ----------------------------------------------------------------- # FORMER SDF DIVISIONS COMPLETE TRAINING The former SDF units are undergoing an standardized education in Damascus to formalize the integration in the ministry of defense as agreed in the integration talks. On October the main forces completed of what became the Hasakah liwa (division) completed their training and the Kobane division started it. # NEGOTIATIONS ARE ONGOING OF A THIRD DIVISION IN AFRIN SDF fighters who returned after the education mentioned how the education focused on what the trainers presented as "islamic values" more than in the technical aspect of the military forces. # VIOLENCE AGAINST IDP With the ongoing return of Kurdish IDPs to their homes, the violence against them continues to increase. IDPs returning to Serekaniye and Afrin are facing violent attacks from mobs organized under banners of "arab tribes". The houses where they return are often looted and destroyed, facing very difficult conditions on arrival. Many of this attacks can be traced to armed groups connected to the SNA, the turkish backed militias that in theory merged into the Syrian army. At the end of October Kurdish refugees returning to Gire Spi faced heavy violence, with attackers beating kurdish IDPs and burning their cars on arrival. # INCREASING TENSIONS IN HASAKAH The neighborhood of Ghuwayran, that hosts the prisons of ISIS fighters and a majority of Arab population, has been a friction point for tensions between Kurdish and Arab populations. Demonstrations to demand that education is held in Kurdish language faced counter-demonstration from Arab population, with threatening actions against Kurdish people often being overlooked if not directly encourage by government forces. # SYRIA FLOODS On October heavy rains in Syria led to floods in Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah, Hama, Homs and Latakia governorates. At least 5 people lost their live due to the floods and The Syrian Civil Defense has carried out more than 300 emergency responses. Homes and refugee camps in Raqqa and Deir Ezzor had to be evacuated. Roads and bridges suffered damages from the floods, as well as power lines and other logistical infrastructure like fiber-optic cable. These floods deepened the humanitarian crisis in Syria, that together with increasing living costs are deepening the hardships that many families across Syria are suffering. # ISREAL ADVANCES IN SOUTHERN SYRIA Israel has been intensifying their operation is Southern Syria, establishing checkpoints and arresting farmers in the Quneitra region. Together with increasing negotiations and military support to the Druze areas of Swueida, circulating reports are hinting at potential operations being lined out on Israel headquarters to extend their influence on Syria. A coordinated advance of Druze forces and IDF in southern Syria could dramatically increase tensions between both countries. ----------------------------------------------------------------- LATE DEVELOPMENTS IN KURDISTAN # CHANGING CONDITIONS OF ABDULLAH ÖCALAN Abdullah Öcalan has been transferred from his cell in Imrali prison to a newly build compound inside the prison walls. The compound serves as an office were öcalan can receive visits of politicians, journalists and state representatives, and is presented as a step on the ongoing peace negotiations. Öcalan is considered now in house arrest in the new compound, from where he is expected to have a critical role in the negotiation process between the Kurdish Liberation Movement and the Turkish State. # GOVERNMENT CRISIS IN KRG Since the election of late 2024, originally planned for 2022 but repeatedly postponed over dispute on the election law, KRG (Kurdish Regional Government) couldn't consolidate a government. After KDP (Kurdish Democratic Party) forced the creation of a unilateral government, PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan) withdraw from the parliament and seek negotiations with Baghdad aiming to access the budget of the regions in their control separated from the rest of KRG. The already tense political situation of Iraq, impacted also by the Iran war and with ongoing debates on other Kurdish disputed areas like Sinjar and Kirkuk, is also affected by the US movements withdrawing it's military forces from the region. Negotiations to solve the current crisis are ongoing, with several Kurdish parties working to mitigate tensions and find some consensus agreements. # CLASHES IN ROJHILAT As tensions between US and Iran continue increasing, with looming threats of intensified return of hostilities beyond what took place until now, clashes between IRGC forces and YRK guerrillas of the Kurdish Liberation Movement are intensifying. After several artillery and drone attacks of IRGC into guerrilla territories, on the beginning of November PJAK announced an action into a military headquarter of IRGC where guerrillas took control of the station for a few hours, destroying weapons an military equipment. PJAK announced the identity of a guerrilla fighter who lost his life on an ambush by IRGC forces, remarking that PJAK is only carrying out defensive operations and won't act on behalf of any foreign forces ----------------------------------------------------------------- Evaluation The negotiations for the integration process of Rojava into the new Syrian State navigated the most pressing issues to avoid a military conflict, but left many issues unresolved, hoping for further agreements and negotiations. Without the urgency that military escalation brings, remaining tensions are being the source of conflicts where civilian organizations struggle on daily basis in the streets. Subsuming military tensions opened space for civil organizing, but the new government of Damascus and it's strong alliance with Turkey leaves very few space for democratic developments. Even with millionary investments of Arab countries and European powers, the economical situation is not improving for many Syrians. New companies and economic institutions are hording the resources that come from abroad, while prices are skyrocketing and many people struggle to meet their basic financial needs. Nearing the two years since Bashar al-Assad left the country, the situation in Syria is far away from stable. The transitional government secured the lifting of sanctions imposed on Syria, its institutions and individuals. It rebuilt international relations through partnerships with Turkiye, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, closer ties with Arab and Muslim countries, and improved relations with the United States, Britain and the European Union, while preserving ties with Russia. Internally, massacres against Alawite population on coastal regions, clashes against Druze militias and harsh negotiations with the Kurdish forces allowed a frame of national unity based on a constrained repression of ethnic minorities, denying claims for a federal Syria more autonomy for ethnic diversity. For the Kurdish people, the relevant processes taking place in Bakur and Rojhilat (PKK peace negotiations on Turkey and US/Israel war on Iran) are having heavy influence on the situation in Rojava. The extraordinary project of over a decade long autonomy is still alive in the imaginary of the people, but the dismantlement of the revolutionary institutions and the turmoil of the region create important difficulties to continue developing the revolutionary project. National unity among the Kurdish regions is becoming a tangible reality as never before, but it also comes with big challenges. Regional instability can still change the course of history in any direction, with events of unexpected dimensions developing every day. Still, the Kurdish question is now a reality being discussed in all four parts of Kurdistan, and extraordinary steps and sacrifices made possible for Kurdish people to overcome the annihilation that brought their existence to the verge of extinction. For us, revolutionary anarchist from many places, their struggle is an example of resistance and determination against all odds. Rojava has become a beacon of hope, bringing important lessons not only about what a revolution needs, but also how to navigate the consequences and reactions that revolutionary transformations bring.
